sources.citation: Ford, Kevin. 1993. A preliminary comparison of Kamano-Yagaria. Language and Linguistics in Melanesia 24(2): 191-202. (Papers from the Third International Conference on Papuan Linguistics, part 2.)
sources.note: For Kamano-Yagaria (not Abaga): lexical tone, two tones (H, L) in some dialects and three (extra-high, H, L) in others; Move alone distinguishes stable vs unstable word-final tones; vowel deletion conditioned by tone; section 3 gives tone correspondences in disyllables (HL and LH patterns in all dialects). No stress statement.

sources.note: Nothing on phonology. p. 972: 'Preliminary work by McElhanon and the author has shown that this language is originally a Finisterre Stock language, but at first sight appears to be almost a Kamano dialect with much of the vocabulary and of the noun morphology linking closely with Kamano, but with some features of the verb structure betraying its Finisterre origin.' Confirms Wurm did first-hand work (the 1970 tapes, work 0) that was never written up.

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. 1975. North-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study, Vol. 1 (Pacific Linguistics C-38), 527-567. DOI 10.15144/PL-C38.527
sources.note: p. 531 lists 'Abaga Language (family-level isolate)'; p. 543 section 2.8.1.3.10 'ABAGA LANGUAGE (FAMILY-LEVEL ISOLATE) (AB), pop. 150' gives discovery (1969), location (Henganofi area, Kose 1, Kose 2, Kanofi), lexicostatistics (25-30% with Kamano, ~15% Finisterre links), bilingualism and classification. No phonology; nothing on stress, tone or accent.

sources.citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 1975. Eastern Central Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study, Vol. 1 (Pacific Linguistics C-38), 461-526. DOI 10.15144/PL-C38.461
sources.note: Abaga mentioned only on p. 472 (as 'the Abaga language of the Finisterre Stock.. shares 25%-30% basic vocabulary cognates with Kamano, and is structurally quite similar to it, except for some features of its verb structure'). The East-Central Family note (p. ~478: 'a strong development of supra-segmental features manifesting themselves in tonal systems and combined tone-stress systems') is about Kamano/Gahuku-subfamily languages; Wurm placed Abaga outside that family, so no statement about Abaga stress or tone.
